explanations.answer: A man's envy of his neighbor
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The Teacher, the writer of Ecclesiastes, says all labor and success spring “…from a man’s envy of his neighbor.” Not love, not hunger, just a long look over the fence. He calls it “a pursuit of the wind,” and I think that means you can sprint all day and still catch nothing.

explanations.answer: A man's love for his family
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, and I'd love for it to be the answer. But that's not what the Teacher says here. He says all labor and success spring from “…a man’s envy of his neighbor.” Family does come up in this passage, just not as the source of the hustle.

explanations.answer: A man's fear of going hungry
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd pick it, since an empty stomach gets people moving. But the Teacher never says that in this verse. He says labor and success spring “…from a man’s envy of his neighbor.” It's about comparing, not about needing.

That's the one, friend. The Teacher says, “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” Folded hands means he isn't working at all. It's a sharp little line, and it sits right next to all that envy-driven hustle, so the Teacher has both sides of the picture covered.

Close to the line, but not the right word. The text says “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh” (Ecclesiastes 4:5). The wise man doesn't take that spot. Folded hands, empty work, and that's the fool in this verse.

I get the guess, since money was all over the verse before. But this verse says nothing about the rich man. It says, “The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.” The Teacher names the fool, and he doesn't mention what's in anybody's pockets.

Yes, baker! The Teacher says, “Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.” Less, but with calm, beats more, but with a fight. I'd put that on a cookie box if the lid were bigger.

Two is more than one, so I get the math. But the Teacher flips it. He says, “Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.” The extra handful comes with toil, and he's not impressed.

Rest sounds lovely, I won't argue. But the Teacher doesn't set empty hands in this comparison. He says, “Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.” The better pick still has a handful in it, friend.

That's right, friend. The Teacher says that though this man's labor has no end, “…his eyes are still not content with his wealth.” He has the wealth and he's still looking for more. That's the part that makes it hard to watch.

This one is True, friend. The Teacher says that for this man “…there is no end to his labor, his eyes are still not content with his wealth.” So the wealth is there, but the contentment isn't. Easy to flip a True and False card in your head, so don't worry about it.

explanations.answer: Who he is working so hard for
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The man asks, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” He's all alone, with no son or brother, and he stops to ask who all this work is for. I think that's a question worth asking before the work piles up.

explanations.answer: How he can earn even more
explanations.explanation: You'd think so, since he never stops working. But that's not his question. He asks, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” He's asking who it's all for, not how to get more.

The neighbor did show up earlier in verse 4, so I see the link. But this man's question is a different one. He asks, “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” He's looking at his own work, friend, not over the fence.

That's the word, baker. The Teacher says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” A man alone, working without end, and never enjoying it. I think that's about as heavy as this passage gets, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

Hard work can be noble, but that's not what the Teacher calls this one. He says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” The man has no end to his labor and no one to share it with. Miserable is the word the text uses.

Working nonstop can look wise from the outside, I'll give you that. But the Teacher says, “This too is futile—a miserable task.” He's looking at a man who works without end and can't enjoy any of it. Wise isn't the word he picks.

explanations.answer: They have a good return for their labor
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. The Teacher says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” After that lonely man toiling for nobody, this is the turn. Two people working together get more out of the work than one working alone.

explanations.answer: They are safe from their neighbor's envy
explanations.explanation: Envy was the Teacher's topic a few verses back, so I see the pull. But he doesn't say that here. He says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” The reason is the return, friend.

explanations.answer: They never have to work very hard
explanations.explanation: If only, right? But the Teacher says nothing like that. He says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.” The labor is still there, and the two of them just get more from it.
That's it, baker. The Teacher says, “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up.” That's the whole point of having a companion. You don't have to dust yourself off alone.
That's a gloomy pick, friend, and the Teacher doesn't go there. He says, “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up.” The companion helps. He doesn't help himself.

Walking past a fallen friend would be a rough kind of companion. The Teacher says the opposite: “For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up.” Two people stick together, and one gets a hand up.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, “Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?” It's a simple picture, and it works. I think that's why this one sticks in people's heads.

It's True, baker. The Teacher says, “Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?” He ends it with a question, and the answer is built right in. One alone has a harder time of it.
That's it, friend. The Teacher says, “And though one may be overpowered, two can resist.” One person alone can lose a struggle. Two standing together can hold their ground.

Forgotten is a strong word, but it's not in this verse. The Teacher says, “And though one may be overpowered, two can resist.” He's talking about a struggle, and about two people standing against it together.

Reward did come up in verse 9 with the good return, so I see where that came from. But this verse is about something else. The Teacher says, “And though one may be overpowered, two can resist.” One can be overpowered, and two can stand.
Not quite, friend. The Teacher says the opposite: “Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.” Three strands twisted together hold up better than you'd think. The answer here is False.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken.” He started with one, moved to two, and then adds a third strand. It's the strongest picture of the bunch.

You got it, friend. The Teacher says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” Wisdom beats the crown here. And a king who can't take a warning is in trouble.

Rich and foolish is the wrong mix this time. The Teacher says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” The better one has wisdom, and money isn't part of it.

A soldier would make a good story, but he isn't in this verse. The Teacher says, “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.” It's the youth's wisdom that wins, not strength.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.” That's a huge crowd behind one person. The Teacher doesn't say why they followed.

The prison was in the last verse, so it's a fun guess. But the text doesn't mention cellmates. It says, “…all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.” That's way more than a cell full of friends.

Guards would make sense in a palace story, friend, but the text never names them. The Teacher says, “I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.” It's everyone living, and he doesn't narrow it down.

That one's False, friend. The Teacher says, “Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” The crowd that followed him is huge, but the people after them won't celebrate him. Fame doesn't last, and this verse says so.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later.” Even a youth who went from prison to the crown gets forgotten by later people. And then the Teacher says it again: “This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.”
